paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 (NSLH1) is a disorder of the neuro-cardio-facial-cutaneous (RASopathy) family. Its features include facial features resembling Noonan syndrome, reduced growth often with proven growth hormone (GH) deficiency, cognitive deficits, and distinctive hyperactive behavior that improves with age in most patients. Cardiac anomalies, notably mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects, are common, and the voice is hypernasal. The distinctive ectodermal features are easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair (loose anagen hair) and darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis (Mazzanti et al., 2003; Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) reviewed 25 patients with the SHOC2 mutation and found a consistent phenotype. Facial features appeared typical for Noonan syndrome and included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set and posteriorly rotated ears, a short webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Patients had reduced growth, frequently with proven GH deficiency, as well as cognitive deficits and distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most of them. Hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow growing, and in 12 patients microscopy of pulled hairs confirmed loose anagen hair. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. The majority had cardiac anomalies, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects significantly overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. The voice was characteristically hypernasal. Referring pediatricians had thought that several of the patients had features suggestive of Costello syndrome or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with the SHOC2 S2G mutation who was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks because of fetal distress. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed rapidly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors considered his cardiac findings and other features atypical for patients previously reported with this mutation.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 boys with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. Four of them had initially been suspected of having Costello syndrome. All 5 had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse, slow-growing, light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles on the palms, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay. They also had unusually long eyelashes, and 4 of 4 assessed patients had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly were each present in 4 of 5 patients. Three of 5 had polyhydramnios and increased birth weight, and 3 needed a feeding tube. Brain imaging showed relative megalencephaly and enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, together with a relatively small posterior fossa, as indicated by a vertical tentorium. Cerebellar tonsillar ectopia was present in 3 of 4 patients. One patient had periventricular nodular heterotopia, a thick and dysplastic corpus callosum, and a Chiari I malformation that developed after birth. Another patient (patient 1) had myelofibrosis at age 2 years without the JAK2 V617F mutation and died at age 2.5 years. This was the first hematologic neoplasm reported in a patient with a SHOC2 mutation. None of the patients had a formal microscopic diagnosis of loose anagen hair.

paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) reported a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry, born to nonconsanguineous parents, who carried a heterozygous SHOC2 M173I mutation. She had right optic nerve hypoplasia, bilateral nystagmus and ptosis, speech delay, hyperactive behavior, macrocephaly (98th percentile), and average stature. Her hair was sparse and slow growing but not loose, and she also had widely spaced nipples and clubbed nails. MRI showed multiple irregularities of unknown significance in the midbrain, pons, and medulla. Her father, who carried the same variant, was tall (6 feet 3 inches) and had intellectual disability, a high-arched palate, sparse hair, and clubbed nails. Neither of them had short stature, a cardiac anomaly, hyperpigmentation, ichthyosis, or loose anagen hair. Their features partly overlapped those of Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, and Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) identified SHOC2 as a candidate gene using an in silico analysis of a protein interaction network. They sequenced SHOC2 in 96 patients with Noonan syndrome who were negative for mutations in known disease genes. Four unrelated patients with sporadic disease carried the same heterozygous c.4A-G transition, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. In 3 of these patients, parental DNA was available, the parents did not carry the change, and paternity was confirmed, indicating de novo occurrence. DNA from several tissues of these patients carried the mutation, supporting germline origin. Among 410 further mutation-negative patients with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype, 21 carried the same mutation, and it was shown to be de novo in all 12 families in which parental DNA was available. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found. All 25 mutation-positive patients had the phenotype previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. In functional studies, the mutation created an N-myristoylation site. The mutant protein incorporated myristic acid, was targeted to the plasma membrane, failed to translocate to the nucleus after growth factor stimulation, and enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) identified a heterozygous c.4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 25 patients with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. The patients were found among 96 and 410 patients with Noonan syndrome or related phenotypes who were negative for mutations in other genes. The mutation was de novo in all families in which parental DNA was available, and no other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found. The mutation created an N-myristoylation site. The mutant protein was myristoylated, targeted to the plasma membrane, and failed to translocate to the nucleus after EGF stimulation, and it enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells. In C. elegans, expression of the mutant caused a neomorphic protruding vulva phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution, in a 5-year-old girl and her father. The girl had macrocephaly, ptosis, nystagmus, optic nerve hypoplasia, speech delay, hyperactivity, and sparse, slow-growing hair. Her father had intellectual disability, tall stature, sparse hair, and clubbed nails. The variant was found by RASopathy gene panel sequencing and was absent from 6,500 asymptomatic individuals. The mutant protein had impaired binding to PP1c. In SHOC2-depleted cells, it only partially restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation and RAF-1 ser338 phosphorylation, indicating loss of function.
